title: Threshold and Parity BosonSampling in the Linear-Mode Regime
authors: Byeongseon Go, Hyunseok Jeong, Changhun Oh
abstract: BosonSampling is among the most prominent candidates for demonstrating quantum advantage. However, while the hardness of BosonSampling relies on photon-number-resolving detection, many experimentally relevant settings and applications instead use binary readout based on threshold or parity measurements, whose computational complexity has not yet been rigorously characterized. In this work, we investigate the computational complexity of BosonSampling with threshold and parity measurements in the linear-mode regime, where the number of modes scales linearly with the number of photons and is most relevant to current experiments. In particular, we establish average-case #P-hardness of estimating typical output probabilities in threshold and parity BosonSampling, a crucial ingredient in proving the classical hardness of the corresponding sampling problems. The resulting imprecision bounds match those obtained in prior hardness results for standard photon-number-resolving BosonSampling in the linear-mode regime. The key technical ingredient is a Fourier-coefficient extraction method, induced by coherent beam-splitter rotations, that extracts hidden hard components within coarse-grained output probabilities. These results indicate that the hard output-probability structure of photon-number-resolving BosonSampling can persist under natural binary coarse-grainings, even in collision-dominant regimes.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the computational complexity of BosonSampling when using simplified, binary measurements like threshold or parity detection, which are more relevant to current experiments than ideal photon-number resolution. The authors prove that estimating the typical output probabilities for these binary measurements remains \#P-hard, demonstrating that the inherent quantum hardness persists even under natural coarse-graining.
main_problem: Characterizing the computational complexity of BosonSampling when using binary readout measurements (threshold or parity) instead of ideal photon-number-resolving detection.
main_result: The average-case estimation of typical output probabilities for both threshold and parity BosonSampling is proven to be \#P-hard in the linear-mode regime.
method: The authors use a Fourier-coefficient extraction method, induced by coherent beam-splitter rotations, to embed a worst-case \#P-hard instance into the coarse-grained output probabilities.
model_or_system: The system is BosonSampling, involving $n$ indistinguishable photons passing through a random linear-optical circuit ($U$). The analysis focuses on the linear-mode regime where the number of modes scales linearly with the number of photons.
key_observables: Threshold measurement probabilities ($T_x(U)$) and Parity measurement probabilities ($P_x(U)$).
important_parameters: The linear-mode regime ($m = \alpha n$ with $\alpha > 2$), and the error bounds $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ for the hardness proof.
main_assumptions: The hardness proof relies on establishing average-case hardness for typical outcomes and assumes specific anti-concentration properties for Fourier coefficients (Conjecture 1 and Conjecture 2).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the basic BosonSampling setup, comparing PNR, threshold, and parity measurements on the output occupation pattern.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the hardness problems for TBS and PBS, then developing the core technical tool—the Fourier-coefficient extraction method—to show that the hard structure persists under binary coarse-graining, culminating in separate proofs for the \#P-hardness of ATE and APE.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum computation models by showing that the hard computational structure of BosonSampling survives natural, experimentally relevant measurement approximations (threshold/parity).

The blue dots illustrate one possible output occupation pattern, where multiple dots in the same output mode indicate a collision. (b) The same output occupation pattern represented in three diﬀerent measurement bases. PNR detection records the full occupation vector, threshold measurement records whether each output mode is occupied, and parity measurement records each occupation number modulo 2.

FIG. 2. Proof overview of Theorem 1. Starting from a sampled threshold outcome x ∼Dm,n with k = |x| clicks, we decompose the clicked set as supp(x) = Q ⊔L, where |Q| = 2k −n and |L| = n −k, and choose an unclicked set E ⊆[m] \ supp(x) with |E| = n −k. Only the modes in L are paired with the unclicked modes in E and rotated by beam splitters B(θ), while the modes in Q are left unrotated. The resulting threshold probability is a Fourier series in θ of degree at most 2N, where N = 2n −2k. FIG. 4. Parity-speciﬁc Fourier-ﬁltering construction used in the proof of Theorem 2. Starting from a sampled parity outcome x ∼Ym,n with |x| = k odd parities, we choose k even-parity modes and apply paired beam-splitter rotations B(θ) to all odd- even pairs. The resulting probability becomes a Fourier series in θ of degree at most 2n. Its top Fourier coeﬃcient, denoted by c2n, ﬁlters out all contributions except those in which all n photons occupy the rotated modes, and therefore depends only on the corresponding 2k × n submatrix UR,[n]. The shared worst-to-average-case reduction procedure is described in Secs. III C and IV.
